name: Elena Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a blasthole drill at the Ridgeback gold mine, outside Tallow Creek. I drill rows of holes, about 15 metres deep, in a pattern the engineers send to the rig's screen, and then the blast crew loads them. Two days a week the rig runs in semi-auto and I watch two drills at once, which I actually love. The worst part is night shift in winter, when the cab heater gives out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life look like outside the pit?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Sami, who teaches at the primary school in Tallow Creek. I'm doing an online diploma in instrumentation at night, and I use an AI tutor every day to get through the maths. I've saved about five months of bills, mainly because we don't go out much. I'm also on the union's women's committee, which mostly means fighting for decent toilet blocks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down, honestly, because I was hoping for better tools, not fewer jobs. At work I'd tell the crew we've dodged a bullet and should push for a pay rise while the bosses aren't distracted. Online I'd post something about putting the savings from automation into wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me, because semi-auto drills are spreading anyway and I'm already one of the people who runs them. My diploma still pays off, because someone has to calibrate the sensors. So I'd be okay either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the instrumentation diploma by the end of next year, using the AI tutor every night. I'd ask the mine to move me onto the automation support team when there's a spot. And I'd keep saving about 450 a month toward a house deposit with Sami.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. I like change, so a world where nothing much happens feels slightly boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use an AI tutor every day. If AI is mostly hype, does that change how you see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, the tutor already does what I need, which is explain the maths three different ways until it clicks. The AI tutor on my phone has taught me more trigonometry in six months than my school did in four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you push for in that pay rise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The blast crew, mainly, because they do the dangerous work and get paid less than the drill operators. Josie on the blast crew has been asking for a hazard allowance for two years. I'd bring that to the committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance if we fight for it, and a disaster if we don't. At the union I'd say we need a training fund written into the next agreement. Online I'd share stories of people who switched into automation roles, because people need to see it's possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me personally. The drill patterns, the shift plans and the ordering go to software, and somebody has to keep the semi-auto rigs and their sensors running. That's exactly what my diploma is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to get onto the automation support team in the first six months, even at the same pay. I'd use AI tools to learn the mine's fleet software, starting with the drill control system. And I'd run a lunchtime session for the crew showing how I use the AI tutor, because some of them are scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a bit of guilt. I know I'm in a better spot than a lot of people on my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, mostly, he's fifty-four and still writes the pre-start checks in pencil. If the checks go onto a tablet, he'll feel stupid, and he isn't. Pete on my crew can hear a drill bit going blunt from the other side of the bench, and no software update knows that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a bit of guilt. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with Pete and do the tablet training together, at his pace. And I'd push the union to make sure the older guys get first pick of the surface roles if they want them. Being ahead shouldn't mean leaving everyone behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public response on the scale of a war, with income support and shared ownership of the machines. I'd say it at the union, online, at the pub, anywhere. I'd say the gains have to be shared, or towns like Tallow Creek die.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a shock, because my whole plan was the screen side of the job, and AGI takes the screen side first in 2028. The drill itself lasts until the robots in 2031, which is weird, the hands-on bit is now the safer bit. My diploma might be out of date before I finish it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd talk to Sami about our money, because her teaching job might be safer than mine for once. I'd switch my study from instrumentation to robot maintenance, the physical repair side, using AI to cram it into a year. I'd put the house on hold and keep the deposit as an emergency fund. And I'd be at every meeting pushing for a fund paid for by the mining companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious, not frozen. I'd be scared and making lists at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the 2-year warning change for you, compared with the slower ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I can't finish the diploma and then pivot, I have to pivot now, half-trained. I spent two years training for the screen side of mining, and in this picture the screen side goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sami say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami would say we'll be fine on one wage for a while, because we've got no kids and our rent is low. Sami would also say stop reading the news at 2 a.m. Sami would be right on both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it, if unions and government work together. I'd say mining companies should pay into a transition fund from now. I'd say it a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is my sweet spot. I finish the diploma, then move straight into robot maintenance before robots arrive around 2034. Screen work goes in 2031, so I'd skip being a remote operator and go hands-on with the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the diploma next year, then do a robotics short course in 2028, paid with my savings if I have to, about 3,000. I'd tell the mine I want to be on the first robot drill trial. And I'd help set up a union training fund so it isn't just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly for the crew. For me it feels doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is spending 3,000 of your own savings a risk with five months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's about a month and a half of savings, so yes, but it's the kind of risk I like. I'd rather spend 3,000 on a robotics course now than spend five years watching robots come and hoping someone hires me to fix them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still buy, maybe in 2029, once I've got the new role. A school wage and a robot technician's pay would cover a small place in Tallow Creek. I'd want to stay, it's home now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real gift, so no one should waste it. I'd tell young people to train for fixing machines, not driving them. At the union I'd say make the companies commit to retraining now, in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd do really well in this one. I can finish my diploma, work in automation for years, and still be only thirty-nine when robots arrive in 2039. By then I'd hope to be a senior technician or training others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the diploma, move to the automation team, and keep up with AI tools on the drill fleet. We'd buy a house in 2028 instead of waiting. I'd mentor two or three people from my crew into tech roles each year, and push the union to make that a formal program.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and kind of excited. It's the one where I get to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people use the ten years as an excuse to do nothing. The mine already took four years to fix the toilet blocks after we asked. If the mine took four years to fix the toilet blocks, I don't trust it to retrain three hundred people without a fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you mentor first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Josie from the blast crew, because she's sharp and nobody's ever asked her to learn anything new. Then probably Pete, if he'd let me. He'd grumble the whole time but he'd do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my plan was built on the screen side, and in that picture the screen side goes first. What would help is free, fast retraining for robot maintenance, paid for by the mining companies, and some income support for the crew who can't switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about who owns the robots. If the robots are owned by the same three companies that own the mines, my town gets the dust and someone else gets the money.

headlineQuote: If the robots are owned by the same three companies that own the mines, my town gets the dust and someone else gets the money.
portrait: Elena, 27, runs a **blasthole drill** at the Ridgeback gold mine near Tallow Creek.
She lives with Sami, a teacher, has about **five months** saved and studies at night.
She uses an **AI tutor** daily and moves first when change comes.
She's **progressive** and pro-union, focused on **shared gains** and older colleagues.
Only the **two-year warning** shakes her, because it hits the screen work she trained for.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her plan relied on the screen side of mining.
whatWouldHelp: Free, fast **robot maintenance** retraining paid by mining companies, plus **income support** for others.
